hooks.text: NASA fired an 820-pound copper bullet into a speeding comet.
Why did NASA smash a copper projectile into a speeding comet?
A copper projectile hit a comet at 23,000 miles per hour.

title: NASA smashed a copper bullet into a comet
description: NASA's Deep Impact mission intentionally smashed an 820-pound copper probe into a comet to see what was inside. The results changed our understanding of where life's ingredients come from.

beats.text: NASA fired an 820-pound copper bullet into a speeding comet.
beats.visual: Artist's illustration of the copper impactor hitting Comet Tempel 1

beats.text: On July 4, 2005, the Deep Impact mission intercepted Comet Tempel 1 with a two-part spacecraft.
beats.visual: Delta II rocket carrying Deep Impact launching from Cape Canaveral, 2005

beats.text: The mothership released a smart impactor for a collision at 23,000 miles per hour.
beats.visual: Diagram of the Deep Impact spacecraft showing the Flyby and Impactor sections

beats.text: Engineers used copper to ensure the strike wouldn't contaminate scientific readings of the comet's minerals.
beats.visual: The Impactor's copper core before assembly, 2005

beats.text: The collision released energy equal to five tons of TNT, ejecting a massive cloud of debris.
beats.visual: Hubble Space Telescope image of the dust cloud after the comet impact, 2005

beats.text: Telescopes initially saw only a blur because the spacecraft's primary camera was out of focus.
beats.visual: Comparison between the blurry High Resolution Imager image and the sharpened version

beats.text: Scientists used complex math to sharpen the view, revealing a vault of organic ingredients for life.
beats.visual: High-resolution image of the surface of Comet Tempel 1 showing debris

beats.text: In 2011, a second mission confirmed the strike carved a crater 150 meters wide.
beats.visual: Stardust-NExT mission image showing the 150-meter wide impact crater, 2011

beats.text: This is why NASA fired an 820-pound copper bullet into a speeding comet.
beats.visual: Mission control team at JPL celebrating the successful impact, 2005

better_than_last: Applied the learning from ep046 by using a mystery structure that builds curiosity about the copper projectile's purpose before revealing the ingredients for life payoff.
